utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Misetic, I see you're ready to continue your cross-examination. Mr. Novakovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony; that is, that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we have to call the case yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think it's not been done. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Misetic could for reminding me. We can't do without each other. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we left off yesterday talking about the evacuation, and I would like to play -- now, first, let me state this: You yourself wound up in Banja Luka on the 7th of August, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall appearing on a television programme in the studios of TV Banja Luka along with Savo Strbac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was either once or maybe twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a clip from your appearance on television in Banja Luka on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this is 1D61-0238, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: TV Host: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Novakovic: First of all, a large number of the members Krajina army are located in there units which have been withdrawn to other territories; that is to say, in their units which had been withdrawn according to our plan, as we said at the beginning. In any case, there are a number of members of the army of Srpska Krajina who haven't taken care of their families, which didn't have an adult family member. You you may have noticed that the tractors, we had used tractors mainly, were driven by 15-year-old girls and even 10-year-old girls. There was nobody else to drive the vehicles, so we had to engage a member of the Serbian army to take care of their family because, as we have said, we wanted to look after the civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am alerted to the fact that the first portion of the video does not appear in the transcript, but I think we can take care of that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think whether we can take care of that later. Have you -- you've provided the booth with transcripts in both languages, and I take it that you will tender these transcripts as well. So, therefore, at least what is said is then part of the evidence, even if it does not appear in its entirety on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that that portion is not of vital importance. Is that understood? It is rather an introduction as to what follows and what is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, there, on the 7th of August, you say that "the units had been withdrawn, according to our plan." What plan?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might conclude that from the clip that we saw, but it is out of the context. I use this word "plan" very often, but there was no plan at all to move units. But everything happened very chaotically. I did say in public that there was a plan, because I didn't want to say in front of the audience that there was no plan whatsoever. So what I'm saying is there was no plan. Everything was done very chaotically. You can see what the audiences were. The audiences were in the -- the Republika Srpska, three days after the aggression. Everybody was frustrated, so I wanted to play the whole thing down in order to avoid panic among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I note you didn't say -- you said they were withdrawn according to plan. You didn't say they fled because of panic and fear caused by shelling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct, no. I used the word "plan," but there was no plan in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it seems to be clear that it was window dressing rather than the truth, what was said on television. That is at least how I understand the testimony of Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you said. What he said at the time, we know that from the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Also, this statement you made in the clip, where you say soldiers were engaged: "We had to engage soldiers to drive tractors" where a family didn't have someone to drive a tractor because 10 and 15-year-olds were driving these tractors. Who engaged these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, nobody. Yesterday, as we noticed, I said that many people left their units of their own will because their primary concern was to look after their families. If shelling was taking place within the territory of a unit, person -- people would normally be concerned about the destiny of their families. All our soldiers had families, and they -- their families were primary concern. Those, who left their units to look after their families, mostly did not come back from their families, and that's why we did not need so many vehicles as we requested from UNPROFOR. We had enough private tractors that people drove themselves, and that's how units of broke up, by and large. I repeat, our fighters, heads of families would leave of their own will to see what was happening with their families. What they found there was shelling, a state of chaos, and they would simply get on their tractors and started moving, even before the things happening the way I described them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, when you say in the video "there was nobody else to drive the vehicles, so we had to engage a member of the Serbian army to take care of their family," you're saying, you actually didn't engage those people. They just left on their own. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac was sitting next to you in that studio, and I would like to play a clip from the say TV programme --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours. I am reminded to tender 1D61-0238 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I know the Defence is planning to play more than one clip from this television programme, as Mr. Misetic has just indicated; and given the witness's answer about the context given, I would like to at least have, for us, the full version of that programme to see if we think there is anything else that is context relevant and we may want to tender. If specific clips are being tendered, I think -- at least the Prosecution is entitled to still look at the whole thing. Then we made decide if we want to raise the Chamber's attention to other portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll play the clip, Your Honour. I don't think that is a basis, though, to say that this portion would be inadmissible, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I did not understand Mr. Hedaraly was -- but it's just a request that when deciding on admission, that the Defence would be invited to give the whole clip to the Prosecution, so to see whether there are any other portions they would like to have admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we receive it this, we have no objection to this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understood you. Mr. Registrar, this portion of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D925 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D61-0237, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. Strbac. "The Croats never intended to live with the Serbs in the former Croatia. "This was now best seen in the latest examples of their aggression in Western Slavonia and now in Dalmatia, Lika, Banja, and Kordun. All of us who were in a position to speak to international officials constantly kept warning them of this fact and spoke of it, that the Croats didn't want to live with us and that we could not allow ourselves to live with them so that the genocide committed against us in the past would not be repeated. I use the term we dare not live ourselves, because it has a stronger meaning than we do not want to live with them. We do not and cannot, of course, live with them and because of this, if it was necessary, first and foremost, that we preserve our biological potential, our people. We could have died off. The civilian population could have been killed. Our civilians and women could have been killed. We need our biological potential for something that is hopefully yet to come. "On the day of the most recent aggression against Krajina, my association, Veritas, wrote a letter to Boutros-Ghali, in which we alerted him with regards to this: A never before seen massacre which would be launched against the Serb population, which is why it was decided in the end to begin the exodus in order to protect the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Strbac says, at the end of that clip: "It was decided in the end to begin the exodus in order to protect the people." That is, in fact, what happened. You and the leadership of the RSK decided to begin an exodus. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. First of all, Mr. Strbac was not authorised to give any such evaluations or judgements and we clarified only too well yesterday that we evacuate only four Northern Dalmatia municipalities, and the municipality of Gracac in Lika. I would like to say that this was not a decision on my part. I did draft a document, but the decision was of the Supreme Defence Council of Defence, and we demonstrated that rather clearly yesterday. The population, as you all know, the population of Kordun and the 21st Kordun Corps was still encircled. It was not outside of the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Therefore, I cannot interpret the statements provided by Mr. Strbac, but they do not reflect the situation. It is a statement that was given two or three day the subsequently. He did not have any competences. He was only the secretary of the government, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with that with Mr. Strbac's assessment that: "We cannot allow ourselves to live with the Croats"? Did you agree with that assessment at the time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always thought that we could live together with Croats and along Croats, but I am afraid that Mr. Strbac is right, that, not Croats, but the Croatian government did not want to live with us. I would not apply this across the board and involve the whole Croatian nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as Mr. Strbac said, you and the leadership decided to "save the biological potential" of the Serb population by beginning the exodus. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a correct statement. It is correct that we decided to protect the population of Northern Dalmatia and municipality of Gracac. In Lika, we evacuated them within the territory. That was our original decision, but things transpired differently as a result of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if in this TV show you corrected Mr. Strbac or said, "No, Mr. Strbac, I disagree with you. We can, in fact, can live with the Croats"; or that his claim that the exodus that had decided, that that was wrong? Do you recall ever challenging that assertion during this hour-long programme?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were guests. We did not have an opportunity to confront each other. There were a few breaks during which we could have maybe talked, but not in the studio in this live programme. You saw that the anchor put a few questions to each and every one of us, and it was really not a place for us to confront each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I tender 1D61-0237 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Subject to the same proviso. In this clip, I know there was, in fact, a break within the portion that is tendered, so I think it is even more important that we get the full version to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was break in the portion tendered or there was a break in the programme, but you observed apparently a break. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D926 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For the record, Your Honour, there is an break, and it is just to save us from having to do three clips instead of two, but that's why it was made clear with a -- a dark screen and then the next clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Novakovic, you testified on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could pull it up, this is page 11.728, beginning at line 23, continuing through 11.729, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, yesterday, in recounting how the decision was made to issue the evacuation order, of which you are the author, you say, you came to Mr. Mrksic's office. "Mr. Mrksic then briefed us on the situation and said, literally, 'President Martic spoke with Prime Minister Babic who is in Belgrade. Babic, as we all know, attended the meeting with US Ambassador Peter Galbraith, and I think that Croatia will not stop.'" Now, I'd like to show you a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation on the 4th of August, 1995, which purports to be between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If could you have 1D61-0177, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it says at the top: "A certain Milan makes a telephone call and talks to an unknown. We think that it is General Mrksic." And if you look at it, it says, a little bit down: "The hell with everything. Do whatever you can." Then: "It's like this, I talked to Galbraith, and based on his words, there is no way they'll stop." Then a little bit father down: "Do something to make this stop." Then voice number one, which is the voice that mentioned meeting with Galbraith says: "Listen, there is nothing that can be done. Pull the people out of there." Response: "All right. We're starting to do with that. "Well, did they stop with that? "Hell, no." Then it continues on down. Somebody else jumps on the line and says: "All right. Here is Mile (potentially, Mr. Martic) He wants to talk to you. "Okay." Then the third voice: "Milan, from the Supreme Defence Council only the General and I are here, so we are thinking of extracting the women and children." Then the voice from Belgrade says: "There is no other option. I talked to Galbraith an hour ago. Judging from what he said, I don't think they'll stop. Conduct every action as planned." Then voice number 3: "So that means that we're extracting, does it?" Answer: "Yes." Voice 3: "Okay. Then we're going up as discussed." Now, Mr. Novakovic, based on your testimony yesterday in direct examination, you seem to have some knowledge of the fact that Mr. Babic was on the line with Mr. Mrksic in the afternoon of the 4th. My question is: Looking at this conversation, looking at the fact that one of the speakers references having met with Mr. Galbraith, when voice number 3 says "Okay. Then we're going up as discussed," can you help us on what that might mean?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the time of this intercept or this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'll ask the questions, but I think you can see very well on the screen at what time the report was prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If he is asking a question about a document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very important; otherwise, I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think if he is asked a question on something that that happened based on his testimony that was for a specific time, I think he is entitled to know what time, not just when the intercept was sent, but what time the conversation was. It does appear on the document below the line "General Staff of the SVK. That appears to me, after the first numbers, to be "04/08/95 1630," which would suggest to, me but Mr. Misetic can correct me, that is on the 4th August of 1995 at 4.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you asked the witness to tell us what something means, and then he is entitled to know what we know about the context. When the report was made it is clear that is 19 hours 20 minutes [sic] ? 927.55. That at least is what is shown on this. But the time of the conversation, could you help us and could you help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly has already testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As you know, Mr. Hedaraly's testimony is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not evidence also done in the presence of the witness, but I will leave it to you, Your Honour, when testifying before the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed and suppress some irritation which is, by the way, understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, let's assume that it's at 1630. Now, that doesn't change what my question is, which is: As a participant in the events in question here, can you help us understand what it means when it says, "Okay. Then we're going up as discussed"?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the timing is important, because yesterday I said that, at that time, I was in General Mrksic's office around that time, in principle. So one might say that at the time I was present. I was privy to that conversation that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. The question was whether you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that when Mrksic had briefed us, he will already told us that Mr. Martic had spoken with Mr. Babic, and that Mr. Babic had conveyed a message that he received in his conversation with Mr. Galbraith. Although, I would like to say that there was Mr. Galbraith's statement that everything had been resolved and there was no need for war, but that's in a different context. After these conversations, we were informed that Croatia would not stop, and that we should evacuate the population from Northern Dalmatia, as I already told you, and from the municipality of Gracac in Lika. This term, "up," "down," doesn't mean anything. It probably means Knin. It is very difficult to interpret these terms "up" and "down," and some other inappropriate words, but this is just the mannerism and the words that people use. Some of the inappropriate words here, this is something that I did not use. Very concretely, where it says "get out of that hole," that could concretely mean that the population should be moved from Knin, in my view. It doesn't mean that this it is really correct, but it would reflect the situation as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Here's the sentence: "There is no other option. I talked to Galbraith an hour ago. Judging from what he said, I don't think they'll stop. Conduct every action as planned." What plan?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Misetic please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that Martic had already called him up before this conversation, and that he had told him what the standpoint of the Supreme Defence Council was and asked for his approval to move the population, because you couldn't move the population from the entire area and the Gracac municipality without approval. So one can assume that he did give his approval for that. I know personally that Mr. Kovacevic, the minister from the same office, called up Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, my question is -- he says: "Conduct every action as planned." My question is: What was the plan?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. The decision assumed there was a plan. The decision stated very clearly what had to be done: Evacuation of the population that was unable to fight in the direction of Srb and Lapac in the municipalities of Dalmatia and Gracac. There was no other plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's look a few lines down. Voice number 1, then, from Belgrade says: "I think I'll call these ministers tomorrow for a meeting with Mladic. I don't know what. "Okay." Where was the meeting with Mladic supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Probably on the territory of Republika Srpska. I can't speculate. General Mladic was the commander of the army of Republika Srpska at the time. So I can assume that, but I wouldn't like to speculate. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And which ministers would be meeting with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either. All I know is that some of our ministers weren't always in Knin. Some of them travelled between Eastern Slavonia, Vukovar, Beli Manastir. They are somewhere in Belgrade, some perhaps in the Republika Srpska, so I don't really know that. I know that several ministers who there were in Knin at the time, and they were people with whom I cooperated closely on the 4th of August, 1995, but I wasn't fully aware of the movement of the ministers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D927 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D106, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, in your statement, you say that the decision to evacuate was not published in the media. Do you recall that in your 2001 statement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It couldn't be published because the media weren't functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a transcript of an interview General Mrksic gave on the evening -- in the evening of the 4th of August to Radio Belgrade. It says -- in the first portion, Mr. Mrksic says: "Knin is enveloped by dark. Evacuation of the population is ongoing. Enemy forces reached at four to six kilometres from the city of Knin." Question: "Does that mean our lines have been penetrated?" Answer: "No. We are maintaining contact. Our forces withdrew to the positions for the direct defence of Knin." Now, Mr. Novakovic, in fact, General Mrksic -- well, let me ask a preliminary question. Your were the -- General Mrksic's officer responsible for information. You would have had some knowledge of Mr. Mrksic having an interview with Radio Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the time, but I was with him for most of that evening; however, I wasn't there when he gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... aware at the time that he told Radio Belgrade that the evacuation was under way?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Yes, it was no longer a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So when wasn't it a secret any longer? What time did it not become a secret any longer?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stopped being a secret, and we spoke about this yesterday, after 1800 hours when I read that decision, and a large of number of journalists were present at the meeting. We told them it wouldn't be a good idea to publish this before the decision was conveyed through the civilian defence channels or civilian protection channels. But when the civilian protection organs had conveyed the decision to their commissioners in those four municipalities in Dalmatia and Gracac municipality, then that decision was no longer a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then, in fact, at some point, you are aware that the evacuation decision did get into the media on the evening of the 4th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was also going to use the Sekulic's book at this point, but given the witness' answers, I don't need to; however, I think this is a good opportunity to, as we discussed yesterday, tender the two chapters of the Sekulic book, which would be 1D44-0003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, two chapters from the Sekulic book.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D928 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm going to take --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With the indulgence of the Trial Chamber, I have a bit of a longer video. This is, I believe, approximately 11 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milan Martic who gave an interview in Banja Luka at an unspecified date, but believed to within one year of Operation Storm. And in this clip, Mr. Martic discusses the events of the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, transcripts have been provided to the booths, and I would like to play the video in its entirety, because it is Mr. Martic speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask whether there is any possibility that we make breaks now and then in playing the video, because otherwise the interpreters may be minutes behind, which makes it very difficult to keep a close eye on translation. So say, for example, after every one or two minutes, you just stop for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video, Mr. Registrar, is 1D61-0240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got one question before we start it. It says "Autumn 1995." You said it was within year --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will actually check on that. This may be more accurate, that it is the Autumn of 1995, I think, based on the context of what he is saying in the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Martic: That first day, the 4th of August, you yourself were present when Knin was bombed along with other places. The Croats didn't have any significant success, other than shifts in the Dinara mountain and the Mali Alan in Velebit. Everything else somehow wept according to its own course; and considering the Croats were in Zagreb that day, especially within the shelters expecting us to react by shelling them, we conclude that there was no need to bomb Zagreb during those initial moments. "What is quite indicative, though, is that I received five phone calls that day from Milan Babic, from Milosevic's office, for one sole purpose which was to suggest that I shouldn't bomb Zagreb. I took this information on record and responded that we should assess what to do at the neglects time. No one from the authorities in Serbia from the regime on contacted me. They simply circumvented me, and all contacts were conducted with General Mrksic. Later on, I saw the name requests not to shell Zagreb. "In the evening at 7.30 p.m., the Croatian Central News Programme was on. We had the generator and electricity within the headquarters. The Croats announced the cessation of air threats in Zagreb because some general of theirs, the cessation of the air-raid warning in Zagreb because some General of theirs - Tolj, I believe was his name - said that all the citizens should leave their shelters in Zagreb because the Serbs supposedly didn't have the necessary range. I subsequently sent General Mrksic the order to bomb Zagreb with all possible means at our disposal and with all the ammunition we had. He replied, 'Okay. I understand.' "Unfortunately, nothing came of this order of mine; rather, to make things even more interesting, they replaced the commander of the Kordun Corps, Colonel Veljko Bosanac, behind my back, for fear that I would directly issue him an order for such an attack, because they disposed of the assets up there. They replaced him and appointed a new guy, so that the order couldn't possibly be executed; and, unfortunately, not a single shell fell onto Zagreb, even though we had millions of reasons to do so. Then the worse scenario took place, which was that at a given moment, during my brief absence, an order that had been written a couple of months prior to in Belgrade was issued, calling for action, in according with orders to withdraw the army, which I wasn't even aware of." "Journalist: On that unfortunate day, the 4th of August, what was your last order as the Supreme Commander?" "Milan Martic: My last order was what I told you about the shelling of Zagreb at approximately 7.30 p.m., when I saw that the Croats were -- what the Croats were announcing. By prior to that -- just a moment. But prior to that, I had passed a decision - unfortunately, I had no one to consult about it - at 1700 hours to withdraw the civilian population from the cities which were under constant shelling, such as Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac. "The order clearly stated that the non-combat population was to withdraw to the villages which were not being shelled, ending with Srb and Lapac, which were in the Krajina and not in the Sumadija. I passed such an order for one reason only, and that was because I remembered Western Slavonia and the massive suffering of civilians there, when I was attacked even by the Serbian regime and all those who conducted different -- waged different politics than my own. This was a mistake. I said that I wouldn't repeat the mistake and withdraw everyone. But all those capable for military service along with myself were to take a rifle in hand and fight for the Krajina. I say that I had no one to consult with, and I gave the order. That order exists to this day. I have it. "Although, later on, numerous attempts were made to manipulate these facts, that this was practically the key, that I passed to the order to for the army to withdraw which later proved to be untrue, because that same evening, I suggested to General Mrksic that we launch a counterattack towards Mount Dinara, that I personally lead the men, as I know the Dinara area well, and that we could surprise the Croats. Upon which, he just stared at me blankly, as if to say nothing would come of this. "I didn't know about this famous order to withdraw the army, nor could I have even anticipated it, considering the fact that the Croats have experienced no significant successes up to that time I believed that the next day would be better for us, to our advantage, and it surely would have been. My absence from the headquarters, which lasted some two hours, was enough for General Mrksic to gather all of his corps commanders, whom he had appointed in the meantime with new men, and to tell them to act in accordance with this new order, which had been prepared by Milosevic some months previously. It was sufficient for me to have been absent for that period of time for this to be issued. My return to headquarters, where I had gone previously in order to set up Radio Knin for it to start function, as a false Radio Knin, had been broadcast and it was deceiving our people. "When I returned, I was confronted by an odd situation. Everyone was whispering about something, those colonels, generals, so that I couldn't hear. But I believed they were whispering about minor issues having to do with command tactics, and I said to myself, It's okay, this is nothing serious. Later, in the evening, sometime around midnight, I asked to get some rest, because I hadn't slept for two days. However, I was immediately received a telephone call from Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik. The lines were still functioning, and they needed to tell me something to give me suggestions, so I couldn't sleep. It was then that Mile Mrksic suggested for the first time, regarding the command conditions which were truly dire, that it was impossible to command from Knin and that it was time to go to Srb. I said that it is out of the question. After a certain period of time, after a half an hour of whispering with some colonels, I suggested that we go to Padjene, a location located above Knin. They said there was an excellent command post there, in the sense that the normal command was possible there and that such tactics would then be implemented so that the Croat would say not be able to find us. I relented then, and said, 'If you're going to Padjene, then okay.' They could barely wait. They simply collected their things, and I didn't know they had previously dismantled everything within the headquarters and they left. I remained with my men sometime until 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning, and left for Padjene where I encountered them. First of all, I realized this was not a command post as they had told me. There was some form of communications system there, but this was not what I expected. But I said it myself, Okay, I guess they'll assemble it. They have good communication officers and things will get better. "Then I asked to go to get some rest, and they immediately provided me with some sort of bed. My men who had accompanied me also rested a bit, and -- sometime around 5.00 in the morning, and we awoke at approximately 8.00. There was shelling going on; however, this didn't bother me. It was a Saturday, yes, but it was odd that there was no yelling going on. Then, all of a sudden, we jumped and saw there was no command located there. They had simply run away from there without even waking me up, which is truly shameful. For sometime we remained there in Padjene; and around 10.00, I went to search for the command. Only then did we realize what I could not have possibly anticipated, when I came across a unit which was in Zitnic, mostly comprised of men from Knin and surrounding villages. "I encountered them towards the end of Padjene and in Kravlja Draga, as we call it. I asked the men where they were going, and they said 'We received order to withdraw.' 'What orders to withdraw? Get back there,' I said, 'the order to withdraw is invalid.' I found their commander, Colonel Davidovic, and asked him, 'Man, what is this supposed to mean?' The soldiers surrounded him and defended him. He was not to blame. He received an order. He was acting like a convict. At the top of Otric, I needed a few hours to breakthrough."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We now appear to have a technical problem, Your Honour. I think the problem is here with the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We immediately get the explanation on the screen what happened. It can't locate a file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A technician will be here to see whether a technician could assist, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, since, apparently, those who are knowledgeable are working on the problem, two matters: The first matter is I got the impression, right or wrong, that there might be something missing in the first portion of the transcript, and I ask for special attention to that, mainly in relation to - let me just have a look at where - somewhere in the middle of page 19, where Mr. Martic says that nothing came of this order of his. I think I heard, following the French, that there was something of an order on shelling Zagreb, but all the equipment available. I might be mistaken, but it is difficult to follow both the transcript and what we find in the video clip as English translation and, at the same time, to follow the French. I haven't got the transcript here. Is it true that something is missing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe you're referring to line 14 there when he says: "Unfortunately, nothing came of this order of mine."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I earlier heard something about what that order was, something about -- but it could be that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I hear something in French that there is with an order using all -- but I might have been lost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have on the transcript that was provided by Mr. Misetic to us, that there does appear to be one or two lines that are not reproduced in the live transcript. It is the transcript 1D61-0240 at the middle of the second paragraph, right after where it says: "I subsequently sent General Mrksic the order to bomb Zagreb with all possible means at our disposal and with all the ammunition ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretations. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry. "I subsequently sent General Mrksic the order to bomb Zagreb with all possible means at our disposal and with all the ammunitions we had." He replied: "Okay. I understand, as they say. Unfortunately, nothing came of this order of mine."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those two lines, I heard them in French and I didn't see them on the transcript. So, therefore, that is now corrected. We don't have to play it again. Have, meanwhile, the tell problems been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then proceed on from the point where we were, and let me just check that exactly. "He was acting like a convict," I see at this moment on my screen, and those are the almost the last words on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was at 8.27.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Martic: At the top the Otric, I needed a few hours to breakthrough. I encountered a brigade from the Dinara. Now you can only guess when they had left, and it was there that I encountered our Colonel Radic. He was pulling his hair out, 'Don't ask me anything, don't ask me a thing,' and so forth. I saw an odd situation. 'Where is Mrksic,' I said. He replied he was Srb. They, therefore, escaped to Srb. I needed a few hours as well from Srpski Klanac. I couldn't break through. I went to Srb on foot, only to find them in Srb, to find the famous HQ which had no command. They didn't even have a telephone. "I saw everything was nearly completely lost. I said, 'Mile, what is the meaning of this? Do you have military police at your disposal. Stop these people. I will address they them.' 'I could see he didn't even make any attempt to,' he said. 'Well, you know, we'll do it in Petrovac.' This was enough of an indication to me that this was the verge of an unprecedented betrayal I couldn't have even dreamed of. It was impossible to think that something like this could happen before your eyes. "Then, during those moments, I was literally on a the brink of a nervous breakdown, not knowing what to do. The people were leaving. No one could stop them. I remained with my associates to the very last man in Srb, until they withdraw. Then I left, not knowing whether the Ustashas had arrived to Licka Kaldrma at Resanovac, in the area towards Drvar. I remained there in the area almost one month after the fall of the Krajina. I think that when I recall these events, I can say, God forbid that one's worst enemy ever have to endure what we endured in those moments. "Journalist: That last day, the 4th of August, how many of your closest associates were with you in Knin, specifically the prime minister, ministers. "Martic: Well, there was no one, apart from two, three of them. I think Toso Paic was in Kordun as the minister of internal affairs. I believe Suput was in Lika. As far as I know, Drago Kovacevic was in Knin. All the others were outside of Knin. They were all somewhere in Belgrade, Novi Sad, and God knows where else. They had important business to tend to. "Journalist: Including the prime minister?" "Martic: Including the prime minister, who went to meet with Galbraith and who signed the Z-4 plan without my knowledge, although I don't know about this. On the day before the attack, Milan Babic accepted the plan without having consulted with anyone, probably only with Milosevic. He signed the famous Z-4 plan. But aside from the Z-4 plan and the guarantees Galbraith gave regarding no attacks, we were attacked. This, too, was probably supposed to serve as a form of deception, the idea we were not going to be attacked, so that we remain unawares. "Personally, with regards to the attack, I must state that no one informed me of the attack, not even from my State Security Services, who had also fled a day earlier; nor General Mrksic, who knew in advance, but didn't inform me. They simply believed I didn't need to be informed, but didn't inform me. They simply believed I didn't need to be informed, even though, naturally, I'm not the type of man that would leave, flee. I would do something prior to the attack to alarm those who died in their sleep, where I personally could have been killed as two shells passed by myself and my children, so that part of the population that did die while sleeping would not get hurt. I would have done something to enable the population to get into their shelters and basements. "Journalist: Do you think they really knew about the attack?" "Martic: They did, they did. He admitted to this fact later on and talked around about how he knew and how he believed that there was no need to inform anyone, and went on to tell a ridiculous story about how he didn't even want to call his driver, so that he could go on foot and so on. I mean, he knew, which he confirmed on numerous occasions to many people. But he didn't feel it was necessary to inform me. "Journalist: We had a news conference that day on Friday, where UNPROFOR Sector South's information chief, Alun Roberts, clearly and concisely said they had received notice at a quarter 4.00 in the UNPROFOR HQ, in Knin, that the attack would anyone at 500 hours. The sirens were not sounded. "Martic: Well, they weren't sounded simply because Mile Mrksic, who knew in advance, so he says, as he admitted to numerous witnesses, that he was told at 3.00. My Security Service, which incidentally fled the day before out of Knin, new much more in advance. None of them felt the need to inform me, for me to have order, or should this have been an order by General Mrksic to perhaps to alarm the people, to sound the sirens, and for the people to take shelter. I mean, we could have at least managed to save those ten, 15 people who were in their beds during the first shelling, as was the case with the deceased Ms. Marjanovic who led the dance school and so on. "Journalist: Many people say that the road taken by a refugee column from Srb to Republika Srpska was cleared two days prior. Is this true? Do you have any information regarding that?" "Martic: Not two days prior. The road was cleared 15 days to a month earlier. It was cleared more for communications, at least that it is what was discussed, to enable better communication towards Martin Brod, which, for economic reasons and for all other interests, is not a bad thing. But it seems basically that the road was cleared due to the fact that a deal made in Belgrade was being prepared. This is clearer than ever that the road was made for this reason, which, naturally, I could not have known. "Journalist: Despite these facts, do you think the RSK, on the 4th of August, could have defended itself? "Martic: I am convinced that regardless of the fact that I have to note that NATO aviation participated in the attack, NATO aviation destroyed our relay systems, destroyed our electric electronic installation systems, because we ended up with no electricity."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The volume is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have a problem with the audio, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I draw your specific attention to the fact that it's not just the interpreters who have to translate but also the transcriber which has, understandably, difficulties in following the speed. We have to verify that both the interpreters and the transcriber is at the point where the video is. Now that the sound is back, let's get it a try.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Martic: As was the late Marjanovic, it was the case of that women who led the dance school and so on. "Journalist: Many people say that the road taken by the refugee column from Srb to Republika Srpska was cleared two days prior. Is this true? Do you have any information regarding this? "Martic: Not two days prior. The road was cleared 15 days to a month earlier. It was cleared more so for communication, at least that it is what was discussed, to enable better communication with Martin Brod, which, for economic reasons and for all other interests, is not a bad thing. But it seems basically that the road was cleared due to the fact that a deal was being made in Belgrade. This is clearer than ever, and the road was made for this reason, which, naturally, I couldn't have known. "Journalist: Despite these facts, do you think the RSK, on 4th August, could have defending itself. "Martic: I am convinced that, regardless of the fact that I have to note that NATO aviation participated in the attack, the NATO aviation destroyed our relay systems, destroyed our electronic installation systems, and we ended up with no electricity. All of this was done by NATO aviation; however, I state that had there not been Milosevic's deception with the famous General Mrksic, we would still have been in Krajina today. We would have suffered more casualties. This goes without saying. "But considering the lie of the land, the possibilities of hindering their advance throughout the Krajina, I am sure the Croats would not have succeeded in taking over the whole Krajina. It is possible that they would have had some success advancement of their front lines, but we would also have had some successes. I must say that we had the possibility of taking over Karlovac, Biograd, and some other places. So how would they have ended up after all this combat? They wouldn't have succeeded had barriers been properly installed within the territory which the terrain allows for. "They would not have been able to conduct manoeuvres with artillery, and their infantry, thus, would not have had any significant success. Therefore, I'm sure that we would have had casualties, there is no doubt, many more casualties than we suffered in this exodus, but we would have remained in the Krajina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had one portion we see and read twice, but apart that, I think we have a complete record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Apologies to the court reporter and interpreters for the extra work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you've now seen Mr. Martic's version of events, at least as he stated them to that journalist. Mr. Martic claims that the evacuation had been planned months in advance. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think many of the things he said were of his own accord, and I was surprised the animosity he expressed towards Mr. Mrksic. I don't think that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think there is a vagueness to the question. We're talking about -- because Mr. Martic talks about both the decision to the civilian populations of the -- and the army that apparently withdrew as well. So if those two can be clarified and not be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- again, this is the second time in front of witness, offering alternative explanations. If there are going to be speaking objections, I would ask the witness be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, if the question is vague and is leading to confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then to explain what is vague and what leads to confusion, that, of course, could be -- I must say, I immediately add to that, that it happens on both sides now and then, but we should really refrain from giving -- in objections, to give further hints, or whatever, to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise for that. But if the witness is shown a 15 minute clip and asked a vague question, Your Honour, I don't think it is a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that what you say is not correct, but it's whether it should be said in the presence of the witness. Now the witness has answered the question. Is there any need to -- it's now on the record, Mr. Hedaraly. I take it that Mr. Misetic has heard your observation and will certainly try to avoid to make any vague references. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me, then, make it even more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, whether he is talking about the evacuation of the RSK military or the evacuation of RSK civilians, he is referring there to some preparation of Mr. Milosevic's, as a matter of fact, he said by name. Correct? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An evacuation of the civilian population and the evacuation of the armed forces are two separate items. It is beyond dispute that Mr. Martic referred to those, but it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is my interpretation correct that Mr. Martic is suggesting that it was military led by General Mrksic who, together with Belgrade, was responsible for the evacuation of the military?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. Martic said that, but that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martic refers to the clearing of the road towards Martin Brod having been done within a month, according to him, of Operation Storm, and suggests in the video that this was part of whatever had been agreed upon in Belgrade. Are you familiar with the fact that the road towards Martin Brod was cleared within one month of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic did not decidedly say that it was because of that reason. It was cleared at the moment when the only link with Knin towards the interior was cut off to Strmica and Bosansko Grahovo. It is well known that the HVO and the HV by that time, by the 27th of July, had reached Bosansko Grahovo. Therefore, the road from Knin towards the interior of the Krajina was no longer in operation, in particular towards the RS. The reason the other road was cleared is because it was already in existence and it was simply made wider, those few kilometres of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you made mention a few times in your testimony about the Z-4 plan and some agreement with Mr. Galbraith having been reached. Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Martic had no knowledge of Mr. Babic having reached any agreements with Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Martic was authorised by -- Mr. Babic was authorised by Mr. Martic to sign that agreement. That was clear. After all, Mr. Babic called from Belgrade about that, informing of that plan from Mr. Mrksic' office. As far as, I know Mr. Martic did not oppose it, at that time or later. As for Mr. Martic commenting on it a few months the later, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Martic had ordered General Mrksic at 7.30 in the evening of the 4th of August to launch a massive attack on Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not quite so. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, when you say "not quite so," how was it then?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present, and I was about to continue. The three of us, Mr. Martic, Mr. Mrksic and I, watched the prime time news on TV Zagreb. When the news were over, around 8.00, the anchor said that there was no longer an air-raid in force in the city, and Mr. Martic's idea was that Zagreb should be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic and myself exchanged glances and did not offer any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue? Actually, I think put the question of what it actually meant. We should go public with our intention to try to hit a target, perhaps not Zagreb it self, but a military target, say, an HQ or the Main Staff. I also asked what the goal of that was supposed to be, shall we achieve something we did in Western Slavonia? In other words, that action was to supposed to justify everything that was taking place. I will try to be clearer. The shelling of Zagreb when the operation in Western Slavonia was taking place --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just let me finish, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It basically served as an excuse for the tragedy that subsequently occurred in Western Slavonia. I also asked them or told them that we had about 30 to 40.000 people at our disposal, and that there was no general agreement on bombing military -- urban targets. Mr. Mrksic then said that he didn't think it would be wise to shell Zagreb. Mr. Martic did agree with that, I claim that, and he no longer insisted on it. I know that for a fact, since I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, where were you physically located when Mr. Martic issued - however you want to phrase it - he says an order, you say not quite an order. But where were you physically located in Knin?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on the first floor in the -- of the building in the office of Mr. Mrksic who was in command of the armed forces of the Krajina. I was there, Mr. Mrksic, and Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, could I ask you to focus your answers very much on the question, so if someone asks you where you were, to tell us the location. If Mr. Misetic would like to know who else were there, he will certainly ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, I'd also like to know why you are present at a meeting between the president of --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- why you are present at meeting with the president of the so-called RSK and with General Mrksic. Why did you need to be present at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an official meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was it a leisurely meeting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the evening, I frequently spent my time with the president and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martic says, in the video, that he had been criticised for not ordering the evacuation in Western Slavonia and says, "I wouldn't repeat that mistake." Now, let me ask you again, did Mr. Martic, in fact, say this at the meeting where he dictated the order to you and you wrote it down? Didn't he mention that he was taking the decision because he did not want to repeat the same thing that happened in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is a mischaracterization. I don't think there is any evidence of Mr. Martic dictating an order to Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, we first raise -- I think it is my recollection that a draft was made and read out, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't want testify and be accused of doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: THE testimony was that it was Mr. Mrksic who gave the instructions to Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in any event, Mr. Martic is present at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There was no audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer was not heard by the interpreters. I think it was in the affirmative. If everyone agrees, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Novakovic, do you recall Mr. Martic saying at the meeting that --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... saying at the meeting that he did not wish to repeat the same mistake by not ordering the evacuation of the -- the same mistake that happened in Western Slavonia by not ordering the evacuation of the population fast enough?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible he said that, but I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to follow up on this alleged discussion that you were present at, where you stopped discussion about firing at military targets. Who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... first, let me tender the Martic video into evidence. It is 1D61-0240.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D929 is, which apparently includes the transcript, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Marko Vrcalj was the chief of artillery of the RSK. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 1D61-00, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Marko Vrcalj was the chief of the artillery of the army of the RSK. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is his Mr. Vrcalj's book that he wrote about these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 9 in the English, please, at the bottom -- actually, the next page. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the section where Mr. Vrcalj says at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. If we could scroll down to the bottom of the English page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vrcalj here says: "In the afternoon when the Orkan commander briefed me to have completed the tasks he has received, I ordered him to get ready to fire to the military targets in Zagreb ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... and Dugo Selo, and that the firing was to start at 0700 hours the following morning." Now, towards the middle of the page in English, in the paragraph that begins, "We headed up towards Serb," in the middle, it says: "Looking at the column of people leaving their homes to go to the unknown, knowing that the Orkan commander has gotten a task to fire at Zagreb, I had to reach the commander to tell him, to tell the guy not to fire at Zagreb. If he was to fire any shells at Zagreb, the Ustashas would lift up their own air force and would mutilate those innocent people." Who passed this order to Mr. Vrcalj's ^ to fire at Zagreb at 7.00 a.m. on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't even know if there was such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... be marked, and I tender it into evidence. I will be using more excerpts of the book, and then we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just seeking clarification that the 25 pages in the English, is that what is being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we got from OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that cover the other portions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you're going to use at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D930 is admitted into evidence. First of all, we have spoken at a speed which was most likely unable to be followed. When the Chamber admitted into evidence the video and the transcripts, that does not appear yet. Perhaps, when corrected, it would appear. But just out of an abundance of caution, I repeat that the video played, and I think it was D929, if I am correct, Mr. Registrar, was admitted into evidence, together with the transcripts. How much time would the parties need, Mr. Hedaraly, to briefly discuss the issue of the photospread? Would further submissions three, four minutes for you be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour, for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we do that immediately after the break. I prefer to do these things before the break because the time-limits are more easily kept, but I'm confident that you will be strict. We will do that after the break. Mr. Novakovic, we will have a break. We resume a at 11.00. We'd like to see you back a little bit after 11.00, because we have to deal with a lot of matters first; that is, the issue related to the photo spread in relation to Witness 3. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we use the time meanwhile. Since now the list of sources has been received, are there any further submissions as far as the two documents, the map and the description, any further submissions on the basis of what you have received; or are you not yet at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to put some questions to him in cross, perhaps at the end. Quite simply, the book he references doesn't match, in some respect, with what he has put on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, going back to the Martic video, he referenced a potential counterattack on the Dinara. Were you involved in the discussions he had with General Mrksic about launching counterattack on the Dinara, on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present when that was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Martic's words, and I'm going to ask you as someone who was involved in these events and afterwards: When Mr. Martic talks about what happened on the 4th of August as being an unprecedented betrayal, he is talking about an unprecedented betrayal by the authorities in Belgrade and the military of the so-called RSK, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he says, but I think that is arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk a little bit about the civil protection, how that worked. You mentioned it briefly in your direct examination, and you were shown some routes for evacuation from Benkovac. So let's start with Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 3489, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is -- this is a document from 1993, January. A plan for evacuation of civilian population. It talks about the buses available, it identifies the drivers, identifies the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says, in case of evacuation, it identifies where the vehicles will be parked, how many people can be carried in each vehicle. Then it says: "If the evacuation becomes large-scale and is limited by time constraints, the closest buses shall be used, namely," and identifies the drivers. And, now, yesterday, at trial transcript page 11.715, at page -- sorry, at line 25, you testified that Benkovac plan was for "a movement of about ten to 20 kilometre," you said. Now, the last line there in the plan says: "There are 100 litres of petrol in vehicles which is enough to cross 2 to 300 kilometres." How far could you get from Benkovac -- let me put it a different way? You could get to Bosnia with one of these vehicles, according to this plan. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably assumed that vehicles should go there and come back again with that fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, just from my recollection of the Benkovac plan, which was with the numbers of cars and kilometres, 25, 25, 30, 35, that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just putting this to you because it is it on my mind, and sometimes I think it's good to know what is on my mind. You have seen that in this plan that calculations were made of the totality of kilometres needed by cars. I was puzzled by it, because how could you add just 25 kilometres and then end up with 500 or 3.000? I gave that some thought; and for me, but if you further want to explore that matter, please do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but just for you to know, if you multiply the numbers of cars and distance, then you will see at the end, more or less the result is that calculations were made on the basis of so many cars, so many kilometres, which would then result in a large -- much larger number of kilometres. That's how I understood the plan on paper. I know that no attention was paid to it when the witness was examined on that plan. But that, for me at least, that caused me not to put any further questions, because I thought I finally understood how the calculations for the kilometres were done in this plan. Just for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I intend to do, just so you are aware, is take the plans and then show you how they evolve over the course of the next two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D931 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... go to 65 ter 2550, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is list of local communes to which fuel for evacuation of civilians has been delivered. Now, this is 30th of March, 1995. Were you aware that these types of lists and plans were being updated into 1995?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you had some involvement, did you not, in evacuation preparation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings where preparation of evacuation had been discussed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I had indirect information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From expert people who dealt with that information. I mentioned Mr. Babic and other people, and it was part of my duties to monitor the organisation of the life of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I had information on all issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask had a this exhibit be marked, and I tend it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D932 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 608, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, this is a document called "Republic of Serbian Krajina republic civilian protection staff." It is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page to page - let me see - it's numbered page 3. The date on it is -- it says, for the place, "Knin," and the date is August 1994. If we turn to the page to the next page, it is the assessment of threats and possibilities for protection and rescue. It goes through in great detail the different types of civilian protection measures that would be undertaken in different situations. So if we could go to page -- numbered page 8 in the English, and go to the bottom, please. It talks about different zones of vulnerability, and that the so-called RSK has been divided in three zones of vulnerability. If we can turn the page in English, it identifies --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Is it possible to have the corresponding B/C/S for the witness as we're moving along, so that he can follow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think the B/C/S, at this moment, matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's an OTP number, Your Honour, so I don't know if there's something wrong with the exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think the page doesn't match. I think it's a matter of combining the two and figuring out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't speak B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I can't help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can get for the witness the portion in his language on the screen which you want to refer to, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 4 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it says: "The first -- the zone of the first degree of vulnerability include the following."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, then it describes villages and towns located in the buffer zone. Frontier villages located within ten kilometres. Villages and towns in the general area of the above mentioned tactical axis. Scrolling down, there is a second degree of vulnerability, which includes towns and villages at a distance of 20 kilometres from the line of demarcation. They would be threatened in the case of initial discuss by enemy forces. Then the third degree includes small enclaves between the tactical axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the civilian protection organised itself by the location of certain villages and areas and their proximity to the front lines. Is that correct, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 31 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say, in your witness statement, that there were no plans at the republican level, but only at the -- the regional or municipal levels. However, the actual civil protection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's page 14 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
